meta.title: Who really said "Give a girl the right shoes and she can conquer the world"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Marilyn Monroe never said it. The line traces to a 1980 Bette Midler remark about footwear; the Monroe credit appeared decades after her death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give a girl the right shoes and she can conquer the world'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marilyn Monroe. Quote Investigator traces the idea to a 1980 Bette Midler quip; the Monroe attribution is a modern fabrication.

answer.label: Not Marilyn Monroe — traces to Bette Midler
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Marilyn Monroe ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator traces the idea to Bette Midler, who told Family Weekly in January 1980, “I firmly believe that with the right footwear one can rule the world.” The now-famous wording is a later paraphrase that only migrated onto Monroe in the early 2000s.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Misattributed to Monroe; modern wording is a paraphrase

source.excerpt: I firmly believe that with the right footwear one can rule the world.
trail: January 1980: the earliest evidence — Bette Midler tells Family Weekly, “I firmly believe that with the right footwear one can rule the world,” per Quote Investigator.
1985: a Houston Chronicle version, still credited to Midler, reads “Give a girl the correct footwear and she can conquer the world,” as documented by QI.
Early 2000s: the polished wording is re-pinned to Marilyn Monroe — roughly forty years after her 1962 death, with no supporting source in her writings.
Verdict: Monroe biographer Michelle Morgan calls it “a fake quote,” and the Marilyn Remembered fan club confirmed it is “definitely a misquote,” per CheckYourFact.
source.excerptNote: Bette Midler’s January 1980 remark in Family Weekly — the earliest documented form. The polished “Give a girl the right shoes and she can conquer the world” is a later variant, and a 1985 Houston Chronicle version credited to Midler read “Give a girl the correct footwear and she can conquer the world.”
source.rightsNote: The underlying idea traces to Bette Midler’s January 1980 Family Weekly remark (an in-copyright modern statement), but the exact popular wording — “Give a girl the right shoes and she can conquer the world” — is a later folk paraphrase with no single identifiable author, so no clean rights status can be asserted for it.

author.name: Bette Midler
author.heading: About Bette Midler
author.bio: Bette Midler is an American entertainer known as much for her sharp, quotable wit as for her Grammy- and Tony-winning stage and screen career. The earliest documented form of this shoe aphorism — a 1980 quip about footwear letting one “rule the world” — comes from her, though the polished modern wording evolved in later retellings before being misattributed to Marilyn Monroe.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Marilyn Monroe
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misattribution: a punchy, feel-good line about shoes and confidence drifted onto Marilyn Monroe long after her death, displacing its real, more recent source.

items.why: No interview, letter, diary, or published compilation — including Fragments and her autobiography — contains this line. Biographer Michelle Morgan flatly calls it “a fake quote,” per CheckYourFact. Monroe died in 1962; the Monroe credit surfaced only in the early 2000s.

Midler’s January 1980 Family Weekly remark — “with the right footwear one can rule the world” — is the earliest evidence, and 1980s versions were still credited to her before the wording crystallized and jumped to Monroe, as Quote Investigator shows.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest reading: the thought is Bette Midler’s (1980), the polished wording is a later paraphrase, and the Marilyn Monroe credit is unsupported.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Marilyn Monroe is one of the internet’s biggest attraction points for orphaned quotations: a glamorous, endlessly meme-able face makes any sassy, empowering one-liner feel like something she would have said. That plausibility is exactly what lets a fabricated credit spread faster than the correction.

In this case the real trail is short and recent — a 1980 Bette Midler quip about footwear — but a 1945-born living comedian is a far less romantic byline than a 1950s screen icon, so the line kept migrating until it settled on Monroe.
context.pull: The thought is Midler’s; the myth is Monroe’s.
